name: Erik Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any AI company, employer, union, party or government, and we don't sell anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a pig man at Thornbury Farm. We've got six hundred sows indoors, breeding pigs for bacon, and about four hundred acres of wheat and barley that mostly goes back into feeding them. My day starts at six with the farrowing house, that's where the sows have their piglets, checking every pen, then feeding, cleaning out, weaning. In harvest I go on the grain cart as well.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I served twenty-two years in the army, joined at eighteen, came out as a corporal three years ago. Thornbury's owner, Mr Pryce, is ex-forces too and gave me a chance. I'm still learning, I'll be honest, the head pig man Dave has forgotten more than I know. But I turn up on time, every day, and I don't moan.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like the routine and the order. A pig unit runs on discipline, same as a barracks, and if you skip a check, something dies. What wears me out is the pay, and the smell that follows you home, my wife Ana says she can tell I'm back before I open the door. She works mornings at the church nursery and between us we just about keep the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. Picture this. AI stays a handy tool, like a better search engine. Hiring, pay and prices carry on the way they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good luck to them, it doesn't touch me. I don't use any of it and I don't intend to. I've got pigs to look after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as I'd say. I don't trust things I can't see working. If it's just a search engine, then fine, it'll stay over there and I'll stay over here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as now. Get my pig welfare certificate done this winter, which Mr Pryce wants. Keep up the overtime at harvest, that's about four hundred extra in a good month. Nothing to do with computers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Nothing to worry about.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you don't trust what you can't see working. Where does that come from?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The army, mostly. You learn to trust your kit only after you've seen it work in the rain. We had a new radio once that the officers loved and it died the first wet night out on exercise. I've stuck to that rule ever since.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your real money worry right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Feed prices, which hit Mr Pryce, which hit us. And the mortgage, we fixed it for two years and that runs out next summer. I haven't told Ana how much it might go up, because I don't know myself.

S0.say: I'd say good luck to them, it doesn't touch me. I don't use any of it, and I've got pigs to look after.
S0.think: I think the same in private: I don't trust what I can't see working. If it stays a search engine, it can stay over there and I'll stay over here.
S0.do: Finishes his pig welfare certificate this winter and keeps up harvest overtime, worth about four hundred extra in a good month. Changes nothing to do with computers.
S0.quote: You learn to trust your kit only after you've seen it work in the rain.
S0.fieldNote: Erik is a former soldier who speaks plainly and values routine and discipline. His distrust of new technology has a clear root in army kit that failed in the field. His quiet worry is a mortgage fix ending next summer, which he hasn't fully discussed with his wife.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now picture this. Very capable AI exists, but it spreads slowly, over ten years or more. Some tasks disappear, but few whole jobs do. Companies hire fewer beginners. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a shame if young people don't get a start. Work is how you learn to be a man, or a woman, I'd say, it gives you a place. Apprenticeships, that's the answer, not sitting at home.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be fine, I'm on the tools. My worry is my boy, Mateo, he's thirteen and he's bright but lazy. If they stop taking beginners, he'll never get his start the way I did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mateo he's coming to work weekends with me at Thornbury from fourteen, washing down pens, so he knows what work is. I'd keep my head down at the farm. I wouldn't change anything I do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, for my son, not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Mateo say about washing down pig pens?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say it's disgusting, and he'd be right. But I'd pay him ten pounds a morning and he'd be there, because he wants new football boots. That's how my dad got me, with a paper round.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should fix it, if firms stop hiring beginners?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Families first, then local businesses, then the government last. I don't want handouts for youngsters, I want firms rewarded for taking them on. Make it cheaper to train a lad than to buy a machine.

S1.say: I'd say it's a shame if young people don't get a start, because work gives you your place. Apprenticeships are the answer, not sitting at home.
S1.think: I'd be fine, I'm on the tools. My worry is Mateo, who's thirteen, bright but lazy, and might never get his start the way I did.
S1.do: Has his son work weekend mornings at the pig unit from fourteen, at ten pounds a morning. Keeps his own head down and changes nothing.
S1.feel: Uneasy, for his son rather than himself.
S1.quote: Make it cheaper to train a lad than to buy a machine.
S1.fieldNote: His answer is family and work first, firms rewarded second, and government last, which fits his traditional outlook. He'd copy his own father's way of teaching him to work. He doesn't want handouts but wants firms to have reasons to train young people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next one. Within 5 years, AI assistants that can act on their own handle most routine office work. There are layoffs and pay pressure in office jobs. Some new AI-related jobs appear, and politicians argue loudly about what to do. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's not the government's job to fix every change. People adapt, I did, I left the army at forty and started at the bottom. I wouldn't post anything though, I'm not on any of that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it doesn't touch me. Office people might have a hard time, and I'm sorry for them, but I've had hard times too and nobody threw a parade for me. Ana's nursery is people looking after little ones, a computer can't do that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. I'd turn up, do the pigs, do the overtime. If Mr Pryce's office girl Sharon lost her job I'd tell him she's a good worker and he should keep her on, if he can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Sorry for others, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said nobody threw you a parade. What was leaving the army like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hard. Twenty-two years and then a handshake and a form. The first six months I drove a delivery van and felt like nothing. Then Mr Pryce gave me a job, and I'll never forget that, which is why I'd work for him till I drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And the politicians arguing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Waste of breath, all of them. They argue on telly while people are worrying about the gas bill. I'd vote for whoever talks least and does most, which is nobody, usually.

S2.say: I'd say it's not the government's job to fix every change, and people adapt, like I did when I left the army at forty. I wouldn't post anything, I'm not on any of that.
S2.think: It doesn't touch me. I'm sorry for the office people, but I've had hard times too with no help, and Ana's nursery is people looking after little ones, which a computer can't do.
S2.do: Carries on with pigs and overtime as usual. Speaks up to Mr Pryce for keeping the office worker Sharon if he can.
S2.feel: Mostly calm, and sorry for others.
S2.quote: Twenty-two years and then a handshake and a form.
S2.fieldNote: His view of self-reliance comes straight from leaving the army with little support and starting again at the bottom. His loyalty to the farmer who hired him is fierce and personal. He's dismissive of politicians across the board, which is a common thread for him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now a faster version. Within 2 to 3 years, AI matches skilled professionals at most thinking work. Lots of office and professional workers lose their jobs. Share and house prices boom. There's a political crisis over who should get the gains. Physical jobs are mostly untouched. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people who've earned their money should keep it, but those who are struggling need work, not cheques. Get them into trades, get them on farms, apprenticeships again. And keep the government's hands off people's homes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think it would get ugly, people angry in the streets. I've seen what happens when a place runs out of hope, I served in a few of them. I'd keep my family close and keep my head down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Mr Pryce for a written contract, I've only got a letter. I'd do every hour I'm given and put whatever I can aside, even fifty a week. And I'd fix the mortgage again before it runs out, if house prices booming means rates move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, closer to anxious. Not for the pigs, for the country.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd keep the government's hands off people's homes. But your house would be worth more. Does that help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not a penny, unless I sell, and where would I go. It might even hurt, if they put a tax on homes. I'd rather it stayed what it is: the place my kids grow up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would church matter in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: More than ever. Our church runs the food bank on Thursdays, and Ana helps. In a picture like that, the queue would be longer, and I'd be there helping set up the tables.

S3.say: I'd say people who earned their money should keep it, but those struggling need work, not cheques. Get them into trades and apprenticeships, and keep the government's hands off homes.
S3.think: I think it would get ugly, with angry people on the streets. I've seen places run out of hope when I was serving, so I'd keep my family close.
S3.do: Asks Mr Pryce for a written contract, does every hour offered and puts aside even fifty a week. Fixes the mortgage again before it runs out.
S3.feel: Uneasy, close to anxious, and more for the country than for himself.
S3.quote: I've seen what happens when a place runs out of hope, I served in a few of them.
S3.fieldNote: His fear here is about social breakdown, which he connects to his army postings. Church and the food bank would be his response, not the state. The higher house price is no use to him and could even bring a tax, which he dislikes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last one. Everything in the previous picture happens, and on top of that, general-purpose robots arrive in warehouses, kitchens, building sites, farms and care homes within 3 to 5 years. Hands-on work is no longer a safe place to be. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say robots in a pig unit is madness. Animals need people. I'd say farms should get a choice, not be pushed into it by grants and supermarkets.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I'd be finished. Pig units are already full of automatic feeders and computers that check the temperature. A robot that cleans out pens, weans piglets and checks the sows, that's my whole job, and I'm the newest man there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do in the first year? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and I don't like not knowing. I'd ask Mr Pryce outright if I had a future, and believe what he told me. If not, I'd try for security work, my army record would count, and I'd ask the church if anyone needs a man. I wouldn't sign on unless the kids were going hungry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. Like being told your unit's been disbanded.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't sign on. What if the bank wrote about the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd swallow it, for Ana and the kids. Pride's no good to a child with no dinner. But I'd hate every minute of it, and I'd be back in work the first day I could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mateo and Sofia?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them Dad's between jobs, like after the army, and we'll pray about it and get on. Sofia's nine, she'd want to know if the pigs are all right. I wouldn't have an answer for that.

S4.say: I'd say robots in a pig unit is madness, because animals need people. Farms should get a choice, not be pushed by grants and supermarkets.
S4.think: I'd be finished. A robot that cleans out pens, weans piglets and checks the sows would do my whole job, and I'm the newest man there.
S4.do: Asks Mr Pryce directly whether he has a future. If not, tries for security work on the strength of his army record and asks the church for leads, and would claim benefits only if the mortgage or the children's meals were at risk.
S4.feel: Alarmed, like being told his unit's been disbanded.
S4.quote: Pride's no good to a child with no dinner.
S4.fieldNote: The robot card produced the expected sharp jump for him, from uneasy to alarmed. His pride about benefits gave way when I raised the mortgage, and he named the reason himself. He blames grants and supermarkets for pushing farms, not the farmer he's loyal to.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The robots one. What would help is a law that says a farm must offer the existing worker the training first, before bringing in outsiders or machines. And proper apprenticeships for older men like me, paid, not a website with videos.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about loyalty. Mr Pryce took a chance on me and I'd stand by him. But loyalty only works if it goes both ways, and machines don't have any. That's what I'd want people to think about.

headlineQuote: Pride's no good to a child with no dinner.
portrait: Erik Lopez is 43, a former army corporal who has worked for three years as a junior pig man on a sow unit with arable land, after leaving the forces with little support. He's married to Ana, who works mornings at the church nursery, and they have two children and a mortgage fix running out next summer. He never uses AI and trusts kit only once he's seen it work, and his views rest on family, church, work and apprenticeships rather than state help. He stays calm until thinking work collapses, worries then about social unrest, and is alarmed once robots reach the pig unit, though he'd put pride aside to feed his children.
biggestWorry: The robots scenario, because a robot could do his whole job and he's the newest man at the farm.
whatWouldHelp: A law making farms offer training to existing workers before bringing in outsiders or machines, and paid apprenticeships for older workers.
